Consolidating Debt Into Your Mortgage

Moving unsecured debt onto your mortgage cuts the monthly payment, and usually raises what it costs you over the life of the loan. It also turns debt that couldn't cost you your home into debt that can.

If you're thinking about rolling loans or card balances into your mortgage, it's worth slowing down, because this is the most consequential decision in this whole subject, and the one most often made for the wrong reason. The monthly saving is immediate, visible and genuinely nice to have. The two costs are delayed and harder to see, and one of them isn't financial at all.

What actually happens

Say you add £25,000 of loans and card balances to your mortgage when you remortgage. Your unsecured payments, perhaps £600 a month, disappear. Your mortgage payment rises by perhaps £130. You're £470 a month better off, and that relief is real.

Then two things follow.

Cost one: you've stretched expensive debt over a very long time

A personal loan is priced high and repaid fast, typically over three to five years. A mortgage is priced low and repaid slowly, typically over twenty to thirty. Moving a debt from the first to the second lowers the rate, and multiplies the number of years you're paying it.

A lower rate over a much longer term routinely costs more in total than a higher rate over a short one. That's the whole trap, and it's arithmetic, not opinion. Run your own figures: the consolidation calculator gives you the total, and the repayment calculator shows what adding to the mortgage does across the full term. Compare the two totals, not the two monthly payments.

Cost two: you've changed what happens if it goes wrong

This is the part that gets left out, and it matters more than the money.

An unsecured loan isn't attached to your house. If you genuinely can't pay it, the consequences are serious — default, a damaged credit file, possibly a county court judgment — but you don't lose your home over it.

Once that debt is part of your mortgage, non-payment is a step on the road to possession. You've converted a debt that could cost you your credit rating into a debt that could cost you where you live. If your income is stable and your job's secure, that risk may be one you're happy to take. If either is uncertain, you've just moved your safety margin in the wrong direction, right at the moment you were feeling relieved.

The honest test. Ask yourself what happens in the version of next year where your household income drops by a third. Under your current arrangement, which creditor do you fall behind with, and what do they do? Under the consolidated arrangement, the answer to "which creditor" is always your mortgage lender.

When it's genuinely the right call

It isn't always the wrong move. It's a reasonable decision when most of the following hold:

  • You keep the term short. If your lender will let you add the debt over five or ten years rather than the remaining mortgage term, most of the lifetime-cost problem disappears. Some will let you; ask explicitly, because the default is the full term.
  • You have enough equity that your loan-to-value band doesn't worsen. Lenders price mortgages in bands according to how much of your home's value you're borrowing against, and crossing from one band into a higher one can raise the rate on your entire mortgage, which can wipe out the saving several times over. Check the band, not just the amount.
  • The unsecured debt is genuinely expensive — store cards, high-rate cards, subprime loans — rather than a cheap loan you took at a good rate.
  • The overspending has actually stopped. Consolidating and then refilling the cards is the classic failure mode, and it leaves you with the old debt plus a larger mortgage. If you're not confident about this, that's the thing to fix first.
  • Your income is stable and you're nowhere near the edge. See the honest test above.

The costs people forget to count

  • Early repayment charges on your existing mortgage if you're inside a fixed period. Often one to five per cent of the balance — on £200,000 that's thousands of pounds, and it can make the whole exercise pointless until the fix ends.
  • Product, valuation and legal fees on the new mortgage.
  • Early settlement interest on the loans you're clearing. You do have a statutory right to settle early, but the lender may add up to 58 days' interest — see the settlement calculator. It's rarely a deal-breaker, but it's real money, and it isn't in the balance shown on your statement.
  • A higher rate on the whole mortgage if the extra borrowing pushes you into a worse loan-to-value band. This is the big one, and the easiest to miss.

The alternatives worth pricing first

Consolidating into the mortgage is one option among several, and it's the hardest one to undo. Before committing, it's worth pricing these too:

  1. A 0% balance transfer for card debt, if your credit file supports it. You pay a small transfer fee, pay no interest, and the debt stays unsecured.
  2. An unsecured consolidation loan over a short term. One payment, no security over your home, and the term forces the debt to actually end.
  3. Overpaying the most expensive debt and leaving the rest alone. Unglamorous, usually the cheapest route, and it clears the highest-rate debt first — see what overpaying saves.
  4. Doing nothing until the fix ends, then reassessing without an early repayment charge in the way.
